metadata.title: Do Factor Strategies Beat the Market? Sometimes Yes. Sometimes No.

summary: Following two decades of skepticism and doubt, combined with worries about a replication crisis in finance, factors such as size and value have re-emerged as statistically robust effects, verified by multiple author teams using larger and more comprehensive datasets than heretofore available. Historical evidence simultaneously shows that even well-attested factors, when implemented as long-only portfolios in the world, have repeatedly underperformed the market for periods lasting a decade or more. This paper counterposes the historical and statistical evidence and suggests an integration.
thesis: Recent academic work has restored factors to their original luster. State-of-the-art statistical analyses using global data have validated dozens of factors in addition to the size and value factors initially proposed by Fama and French. Concerns that factor outperformance had been arbitraged away after publication have been put to rest.
key_takeaways: Recent academic work has restored factors to their original luster. State-of-the-art statistical analyses using global data have validated dozens of factors in addition to the size and value factors initially proposed by Fama and French. Concerns that factor outperformance had been arbitraged away after publication have been put to rest.

Academic work uses long-short factors free of transaction costs and margin interest. Most investors who pursue factor strategies in the world are limited to long-only portfolios that do incur transaction costs. The historical record shows recurring periods of sustained factor under-performance for such long-only portfolios.

The paper reconciles the statistical evidence with investor experience to sound a cautionary note for portfolio managers. A positive monthly mean obtained over many decades, using long-short portfolios, is quite compatible with periods of lagging performance by long-only portfolios that can persist for arbitrarily long periods.
